lines.trans: Come with me into my office.
Chef, where are we going now?
We need a very serious conversation.
Did you hear everything in the kitchen?
I heard every word of yours.
I myself do not understand anything.
You caused a real big scandal.
I did not want to offend anyone.
Go into the room and close the door.
Good, I am already closing the door.
Sit on a chair and listen to me.
I am listening to you attentively, chef.
Now your life will change greatly.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('big, large').

examples.text: Аракелян просит время. Сумма очень большая.
examples.trans: Arakelyan is asking for more time. The sum is very large.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: И, Марина Сергеевна, читайте всё внимательно! Особенно мелким шрифтом!
examples.trans: And, Marina Sergeyevna, read everything carefully! Especially in fine print!

meanings.note: ends a conversation or an order: 'Всё, свободен' = that's all, you can go
Secondary conversational sense ('that's it, done') (at the start of a sentence) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'door' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The door is behind the wardrobe.
Open the door. Is this flat nine?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.

Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'крывать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to close', forming an aspectual pair with 'закрыть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to turn a blind eye') ('закрывать глаза на' + accusative) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: А я глаза на это закрывать не буду. Я подниму людей!
examples.trans: Well, I'm not going to close my eyes to this. I'll rally people!

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'крыть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to close', forming an aspectual pair with 'закрывать'.

examples.text: А потом, Аркадий Борисович, мы закроем ваше дело.
examples.trans: And then, Arkady Borisovich, we will close your case.

заходить.gloss: to come in, to drop in

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'ходить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to come in', forming an aspectual pair with 'зайти'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to drop in') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Не стой в дверях, смелее заходи ко мне в кабинет!
examples.trans: Do not stand in the doorway, come on into my office boldly!

examples.text: После работы мы часто заходим выпить кофе в соседний бар.
examples.trans: After work we often drop in to drink coffee at the neighboring bar.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'пойти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (to run for a second term) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: reflexive: the thing itself changes

examples.text: Узнаёшь? У нас здесь ничего не изменилось.
examples.trans: Recognise it? Nothing has changed here.

meanings.note: From French 'cabinet' (private study or office).

examples.text: Николай Филиппович, я сейчас в кабинете у мэра.
examples.trans: Nikolai Filippovich, I'm in the mayor's office right now.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'every', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'room', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'where'.

examples.trans: Wait, where are you two going?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'стоящий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('real, genuine').
Secondary conversational sense ('present, current') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ваня, да пойми ты наконец! Это настоящий успех.
examples.trans: Vanya, understand at last! This is real success.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
needs 'не' with the verb: никто не войдёт

examples.trans: I know the town like nobody else.

examples.text: Садитесь и держите дверь. Никто не войдёт.
examples.trans: Sit down and hold the door. Nobody will come in.

meanings.note: usually in the genitive ничего, with не: ничего не осталось

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: short form 'нужен / нужна / нужно / нужны' + dative: 'мне нужна работа' = I need a job

meanings.en: to offend, to hurt someone's feelings
meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'идеть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to offend, to hurt', paired with 'обижать'.

examples.trans: Sorry, I didn't mean to offend you.
He didn't want to offend anyone.

examples.text: Извини, я не хотела обидеть. А ты что здесь делаешь?
examples.trans: Sorry, I didn't mean to offend you. And what are you doing here?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'идти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: понимаешь? = you know? do you understand?

examples.trans: I want to go to the sea, you know?

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: Agentive or instrument masculine noun meaning 'conversation', declining across all six Russian grammatical cases.

examples.text: У нас с тобой серьёзный разговор.
examples.trans: You and I have a serious talk to have.

examples.text: Есть интересный разговор. Всё хорошо, малыш.
examples.trans: There's an interesting conversation. Everything is fine, kid.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'serious' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('important, weighty, influential') (серьёзный человек) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я приехала к очень серьёзному человеку.
examples.trans: I have come to see a very important man.

examples.text: Я приехала к очень серьёзному человеку. Он меня ждёт.
examples.trans: I have come to see a very important man. He is waiting for me.

meanings.en: to sit down, to take a seat
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'есть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to sit down', paired with 'садиться'.

examples.trans: He sat down on a chair.
Listen, sit down. Sit down, please.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'strongly'.

examples.trans: The wind is blowing hard outside.

examples.text: Я так два года потеряла. Любила так сильно!
examples.trans: I lost two years like that. I loved him so much!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'scandal', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: A scandal began in the restaurant dining room.
There is no need to make a scene.

examples.text: Если шеф увидит нож, будет скандал!
examples.trans: If the chef sees the knife, there will be a scandal!

meanings.note: 'дать слово' = to give one's word, 'держать слово' = to keep one's word
'дать слово' = to give one's word, 'держать слово' = to keep one's word

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to listen', forming an aspectual pair with 'послушать'.
the imperative 'слушай' starts a sentence, like 'look, ...'
Secondary conversational sense ('hello (on the phone)') ('Слушаю' = I'm listening) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лышать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to hear', forming an aspectual pair with 'услышать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to hear about') (слышать о + prepositional) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Как странно, я ничего об этом не слышал.
examples.trans: How strange, I've heard nothing about it.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'chair', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Put the chair by the table.

examples.text: А зачем нам бревно? Я вот стулья взял!
examples.trans: And why do we need a log? I brought folding chairs right here!

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.en: to arrange, organize, set up an event or scheme
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'строить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to arrange', forming an aspectual pair with 'устраивать'.

examples.text: Я всё устрою на высшем уровне.
examples.trans: I will arrange everything at the highest level.
They organized a party for friends.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'well'.
Secondary conversational sense ('good, fine') (as an answer) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Хорошо, Виктор Петрович, я сейчас же всё переделаю заново!
examples.trans: All right, Viktor Petrovich, I will redo everything right now!

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
